Albuquerque at a glance for a seller

New Mexico's biggest city is also the Bernalillo County seat, with 564,559 people in the 2020 census. The Rio Grande runs through a basin that has the Sandia Mountains on its eastern edge and the West Mesa to the west. Houses by the river and houses in the foothills can vary in age, lot type and weather exposure, even in the same ZIP code.

Your bill is tied to the parcel, so the neighborhood name tells you little. Two houses on nearby blocks may belong to different taxing districts.

Who bills property tax in Albuquerque?

Albuquerque addresses get their property tax bill from the Bernalillo County Treasurer, who also collects it, while the county Assessor determines the value. The city itself mails no property tax bill.

Each year the state Department of Finance and Administration sets county rates in September, the Assessor hands the tax roll to the Treasurer by October 1, and bills follow, normally by November 1 or the next business day if that is a weekend.

The Treasurer is at 415 Silver Ave SW downtown, phone (505) 468-7031. Value questions go to the Assessor in the same building, (505) 222-3700.

Property tax dates

You pay half by November 10 and half by April 10. Penalties start on December 10 for the first half and on May 10 for the second.

DateWhat happens
January 1Value is fixed for the year and assigned to the owner of record
April 1Last day for the Assessor to mail Notices of Value
30 days after mailingDeadline for protests and exemption applications
October 1Tax roll goes from Assessor to Treasurer
November 1Bills go out by mail and online
November 10First half due
December 10Late fees begin on the first half
April 10Second half due
May 10Late fees begin on the second half

Confirm any date with the Treasurer before you rely on it, since a deadline that lands on a weekend can shift. Sellers should focus on the November and April payments. Ask the title company how the current half will be split with the buyer, and hold on to your payment confirmations as proof.

What happens if tax goes unpaid

Each month a balance stays unpaid, it gains 1% interest, and a separate 1% penalty accrues too. The penalty stops at 5% and has a $5 floor.

Owners remain liable even if no bill arrives. Many bills come back undelivered after the November mailing, mostly because of outdated mailing addresses, so keep the addresses for your Notice of Value and your bill current. Someone who has left an inherited or rented house is the likeliest to miss a bill.

In June the Treasurer mails delinquent notices. An owner who cannot pay everything at once can call the Treasurer to arrange payments, and a monthly plan is available.

Protesting your value and lowering the bill

You have 30 days from the mailing of the Notice of Value to protest the valuation with the Assessor, and several savings programs use the same 30 days. Protests can be filed through the Assessor's online portal or at the counter, 415 Silver Ave SW. An informal talk with a field appraiser comes first. If the value stays disputed, the Protest Valuation Review Board holds a hearing. After a missed window, the remaining route is to pay first, then ask for a refund through the Second Judicial District Court, 400 Lomas Blvd NW, which charges a $132 filing fee.

Savings programs worth asking about:

  • Head of Family: $2,000 off taxable value, limited to a single property in the state for each household.
  • Veteran exemption: as much as $10,000 off taxable value, backed by a certificate from the state's service commission.
  • Value freeze: open to owners 65 or older earning no more than $42,900 in modified gross income, or disabled owners earning $41,900 or less. It locks the assessed value, though the rate can still change.

There is no homestead exemption in New Mexico. Taxable value is a third of assessed value, and the Head of Family and veteran reductions are taken from that third.

Public improvement districts

Some Albuquerque subdivisions carry a public improvement district, or PID, which adds a line to the tax bill that pays back bonds for neighborhood infrastructure. The amount per parcel changes from year to year, parcel size and other factors affect it, and a buyer continues the remaining bond payments where the seller left off. An owner may pay a PID off early, and the only exemption on PID payments is the 100% disabled veteran waiver.

Owners inside a district should say so to the buyer and title company at the start. A cash buyer will fold the remaining balance into the offer, and knowing your payoff figure prevents a surprise at the closing table. The county Assessor keeps a page listing the name and boundary of each district.

Short-term rental permits

If the house was ever rented by the night, the city's permit rules apply, and the city does enforce them. Any dwelling, or part of one, let for fewer than 29 consecutive days is a short-term rental.

The permit needs a business license, a floor plan, proof of insurance of at least $250,000 per unit, and a posted Good Neighbor Agreement. The fee is $120 in the first year and $90 for renewals. Operators must also file a monthly lodgers' tax report by the 25th, even when a platform remits the tax. Skipping the permit risks fines and a bar on operating later, so resolve any unpermitted rental history before you put the house on the market.

Notices of Value and the seller's timeline

The Assessor values a property as it stands on January 1 and charges it to whoever is the owner of record that day. Notices of Value go out by April 1, which starts the 30-day period for protests and exemption applications. A spring sale still carries that notice, so tell the buyer and settle in the contract who will file a protest.

When a house passed to an heir without a new deed, mail still goes to the owner of record. Update the record before listing so notices reach someone who can respond.

Common snags when selling

Paperwork, not buyers, causes most Albuquerque delays. These come up often:

  • A bill mailed to a former address that is now delinquent.
  • A PID balance that was not known until the title search.
  • An unfinished addition that changes the assessed value, or an unpermitted rental.
  • A deed that never moved into an heir's name after a death.

Under any sale route, the title company pays leftover tax out of your proceeds at closing. Look up your balance in the Treasurer's online tax search first. A cash buyer purchasing as is can absorb many of these problems, but will still ask for that number.

You pick the closing dateClose in as little as 7 days or on the date that works for you, with no fees or commissions.Get My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

Does the City of Albuquerque send its own property tax bill?

No. Bernalillo County bills Albuquerque property owners. The Assessor sets the value, the Treasurer mails the bill and collects, and the state sets the rates each September.

When is Albuquerque property tax due?

Half is due November 10 and half is due April 10. Late fees begin December 10 on the first half and May 10 on the second half.

How much are the late fees on Albuquerque property tax?

Interest is 1% of the unpaid tax each month, and the penalty is 1% each month up to 5%, with a $5 minimum penalty.

Can I sell my Albuquerque house if I still owe property tax?

Yes. The unpaid tax, with any penalty and interest, is normally paid from the sale proceeds by the title company at closing. Check the exact balance with the Bernalillo County Treasurer first.

Is there a homestead exemption in Albuquerque?

No. New Mexico has no homestead exemption. The Assessor offers Head of Family, which reduces taxable value by $2,000, plus veteran exemptions and a value freeze for qualifying owners.

Last updated November 14, 2026.

Behind on Santa Fe property tax?

Get My Cash Offer →

Who sends the bill

Santa Fe sits in the Northern Rio Grande Valley at about 7,000 feet above sea level. The bill does not come from City Hall. In New Mexico the county runs the process. A Santa Fe homeowner therefore deals with two Santa Fe County offices, one that puts a number on the house and one that sends the invoice and takes payment.

QuestionOfficeDetails
Who values my house?Santa Fe County AssessorMails a Notice of Value yearly, usually near April 1
Who bills and collects?Santa Fe County TreasurerExpect the bill around Halloween
Where do I pay?Treasurer, 100 Catron St.Online portal, phone, mail (P.O. Box T, Santa Fe, NM 87504) or in person
Who hears a value appeal?County Valuation Protest BoardThree members, one from the State Property Tax Division

Due dates and late charges

First-half tax goes delinquent after December 10, with charges starting on the 11th, and the second half has until May 10. Read the due date printed on your own bill before scheduling a closing, and use the Treasurer's page to confirm.

If a payment is late:

  • Interest begins on the thirtieth day after the due date at 1 percent per month or partial month, which adds up to 12 percent a year (Section 7-38-49 NMSA 1978).
  • A separate penalty of 1 percent of the unpaid tax accrues each month or partial month and stops at 5 percent.
  • Where the penalty would come to under five dollars, it is five dollars.

Ask the Treasurer about a monthly payment plan. The online portal shows each bill with ten years of tax history. Paying by card adds a 2.5 percent fee, and an e-check adds just $1.95.

How the Assessor sets your value

Appraisals happen every year at the Assessor's office. The figure on your notice reflects the prior year's market value, so it trails the market a little. If you sold or refinanced recently, an appraiser may already hold your price on file.

Residential property has a ceiling. State law holds a house, apartment or manufactured home to a 3 percent yearly rise over the prior year's assessed value. One third of the appraised value becomes the taxable value, and the rate is multiplied against it.

This ceiling matters at sale time because it protects only the current owner. A change of ownership ends it, and the property is then assessed at market value. That includes a transfer between an LLC and its members, as the New Mexico Court of Appeals decided in Giddings v. SRT Mountain Vista, LLC. A buyer of a long-held Santa Fe house can therefore receive a larger bill than you paid.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How to appeal your assessment

Mail or file the petition at the Assessor's office within a month of the date stamped on the Notice of Value, meaning 30 days. Notices typically go out on or around April 1, and in some years the date moves, with the deadline moving along with it.

  1. An appraiser reviews the property on site, taking photos, checking the exterior and correcting data. The appraiser then writes to tell you whether the value changed.
  2. If you still disagree, you may be invited to an informal conference where you can bring comparable sales and other evidence.
  3. If that fails, a formal hearing is held before the County Valuation Protest Board, with certified-mail notice at least 15 days before. A written ruling follows within 30 days.

The law sets 180 days from filing to resolve a protest, though the State Property Tax Director may extend it. Bring five copies of every document, and hand the appraiser a copy at least 30 days ahead of the hearing. Skip the hearing and you lose by default. Filing online through the Assessor's portal is also an option.

Exemptions

Four exemptions can shrink a Santa Fe County bill. Each must be claimed in the 30 days after the Notice of Value is mailed.

  • Head of Family: $2,000 off the taxable value of residential real estate. Only one person per household can claim it, and only in one county in the state.
  • Veteran: a $4,000 reduction for an honorably discharged veteran or an unmarried surviving spouse who holds a certificate of eligibility from the state's veteran services department. It stays on the property until ownership changes, and it must be claimed in person.
  • 100 percent disabled veteran: a full exemption on the residence, again lasting until ownership changes.
  • Valuation freeze: open to owners aged 65 and up, or permanently disabled, whose modified gross income is $41,900 or less. Proof of income and age or disability is required.

Several of these end at transfer, so the buyer must apply fresh. You have nothing to file as the seller, but a reduced bill does not travel with the house.

Historic districts and short-term rentals

Parts of town fall inside historic districts. Santa Fe has several, among them the Don Gaspar Area, Westside-Guadalupe, Historic Transition and Historic Review districts. Changes to the outside of a building there go through the city's Historic Preservation Division and the Historic Districts Review Board, so allow extra time.

If you plan repairs before selling, such as new windows, stucco or a roofline change, ask the Historic Preservation Division at 505-955-6605 whether the property is in a district first. A cash buyer taking the house as-is spares you that review.

Short-term rentals are also regulated. Anyone who owns or operates one in calendar year 2026 must hold an STR permit plus a city business license. If the house has been a rental, confirm the permit is current, since it shapes what the next owner may do.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed

Ask the Treasurer for a payoff, and the closing agent will settle it out of what you receive. The title company checks the county record, subtracts the balance and forwards that amount to the Treasurer.

  • Download the current bill and the ten-year history from the Treasurer's portal.
  • Ask whether interest and penalty are running, using the 1 percent monthly rules above.
  • Make sure any protest you filed is settled, or tell the buyer it is still open.
  • Tell your buyer if an exemption or valuation freeze will end at transfer.

When back tax is what is pushing you to sell, a cash sale with no repairs can close on a timeline that fits the debt. Any offer depends on the house, so no price is promised here. Before you call anyone, print the Treasurer's ten-year history and the latest Notice of Value so you can answer questions about both on the spot, and write down whether an exemption or a protest is active.

Frequently asked questions

When are Santa Fe property taxes due?

The first half goes delinquent after December 10, with charges beginning on the 11th, and the second half has until May 10. Confirm the date printed on your bill.

Does the City of Santa Fe collect property tax?

No. The Santa Fe County Assessor sets the value and the Santa Fe County Treasurer bills and collects it. Both offices are county offices.

How long do I have to protest my Santa Fe value?

You have 30 days from the official mailing date of the Notice of Value. Notices typically go out on or around April 1, but the date can shift in a given year.

What is the penalty on late Santa Fe property tax?

Interest of 1 percent a month starts on day thirty after the due date, and a 1 percent monthly penalty is added until it reaches 5 percent.

Does the 3 percent cap on increases follow the house to a buyer?

No. A change of ownership ends the limit on a residential property, and the house is then assessed at market value.
